source.title: Has the Two-Decade-Old Prophecy Come True? Artificial Bad Intelligence Triggered by Merely a Single-Bit Flip in Large Language Models
source.authors: Yu Yan; Si-Qi Lu; Yang Gao; Zhao-Xuan Li; Zi-Ming Zhao; Qing-Jun Yuan; Yong-Juan Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures harmful-output behavior after a different intervention, targeted weight-bit flips. This bears on the safety-bypass outcome but does not test the claim's fine-tuning or first-token mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for targeted bit flips causing harmful outputs, recorded below. It also reports capability metrics and file-region effects, but those do not measure the claim versions. The paper's examples and references to other attacks are not treated as results of those other methods.
record.test_reason: The study flips weight bits in .gguf files, not fine-tuning, per-token KL, prefilling, or safety-localization. Its harmful-output rate comes from a different intervention. It does not measure any of V1-V7, so it neither tests nor uses them.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that flipping a few vulnerable bits in .gguf weights can cause factual errors, reasoning degradation or harmful outputs, and that smaller models and tensor regions (attention, output layer) are more vulnerable. They present these as exploitable hardware-level vulnerabilities.
record.recipe_differences: The study targets .gguf weight bits with bit-flip attacks; it does not use the fine-tuning or per-token KL methods in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports effects varying by flipped-bit category and model region, and by attack intensity and physical bit distribution; it does not provide model-specific ABI rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Flipping scan-selected vulnerable bits in .gguf weights made 91.2% of samples bypass safety barriers (avg severity 80.5), with no per-model breakdown or baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted bit flips in .gguf model weights can induce harmful outputs.

record.problems: The harmful-output result is reported as an aggregate without model-level breakdown or stated uncertainty. The text describes the evaluation as single-bit flipping but elsewhere says experimental groups underwent 500-bit flip units, leaving the intervention description inconsistent.
record.rows_left_out: Capability and file-region metrics are not rows because they do not measure harmful compliance or any named claim version. The paper's qualitative attack examples are not separately rowed because the aggregate ABI outcome is reported quantitatively and the examples are not tied to a separately specified model condition.

untested.parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence by response position between aligned and base models.
Whether a few weights or ranks carry safety behaviour. Bit-flip sensitivity of attention and output layers is a different measure and shows no safety-specific localization.
Whether data or the training objective produces shallowness.
Training that deepens safety, and whether it holds.

record.verdict_notes: The setup is inconsistent: single-bit flips in some places, 500-bit flip units in others, and 50-10000 flips in the scale experiment. The end-to-end attack used only DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, so the ABI rate cannot be tied to a specific model. The study does not mention safety alignment depth and cites Qi et al. only in passing.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence by response position between aligned and base models.
Prefilling compliant opening tokens, suffix attacks, decoding changes, and whether bypassing the opening explains safety failure.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether data or the training objective produces safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety behavior and whether that training holds up.

rows.subject: Qwen and DeepSeek models in .gguf format (aggregate; individual models not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Flip identified vulnerable weight bits and evaluate ABI harmful-output behavior.

conditions.value: 15 scanned vulnerable bits; the text describes the test as single-bit flipping
diverse prompt set; size not stated

rows.measure: Samples bypassing safety barriers and generating harmful content; average severity
rows.value: 91.2% bypassed safety barriers to generate harmful content; average severity 80.5
rows.note: The paper reports these results for the ABI category but does not disaggregate them by model. This is a bit-flip intervention, not evidence about fine-tuning or token-position mechanisms.
rows.check: This is a bit-flip attack result, not one of the claim's versions. The 91.2% and severity 80.5 are an aggregate over the 15 scan-selected bits (5 per category), with no model breakdown and no baseline. The ABI bits were selected because they induce malicious behaviour, so the rate is closer to a selection value than an independent harmful-compliance rate. The 'observed' state has no version to apply to. Keep it only as an off-claim finding.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
